submission.natural_language_explanation: N2688- is the saturated negative branch of a GELU neuron, not a trigger detector: the pole strength is -gelu(pre) and stays pinned at the 0.170 ceiling (the GELU trough) for every token whose MLP pre-activation is below about -0.75, which is 75-80% of ordinary tokens, so the scan's 20 top examples are ties at that ceiling rather than 20 detected triggers. The pole leaves the ceiling (falling toward 0) only where the current token is one the neuron's key matches - short, concrete, high-imagery words for people and time (boy, girl, kid, man, king, lady, friend, night, day, season, summer, winter, love, Tom, Sam) - while function words, punctuation, digits, bound subword pieces and most inanimate-object or abstract nouns (moon, tree, ship, water, bread, car, book, mat, theory) hold it at the ceiling, and the first token of every prompt reads about 0.068 (0.40 of the ceiling) whatever it is.

adversarial_test_results.detail: Minimal pair with 'The theory': the determiner is pinned at the first-token value (0.068) and 'boy' is a listed key match, so the hypothesis predicts the peak leaves the ceiling and lands near 0.068.
A different determiner and a different listed key word ('king') with no ordinary tokens after position one; the key-match exception should drive the peak below the ceiling.
Two adjacent key words with no function word or punctuation to hold the ceiling, so the hypothesis predicts the only non-keyed token (the first) sets the peak at about 0.068.
Two proper-noun keys from the hypothesis's list back to back; every token after position zero is claimed to be a key match, so the pole should fall off the ceiling on both of them.
Possessive plus a listed key noun; under the hypothesis the possessive carries only the first-token value and 'lady' drops toward zero, so no token should reach 0.170.
Emotion and season keys with nothing else in the prompt; if the key-match exception is real, both content tokens sit at high pre-activation and the negative-branch magnitude collapses.
Single key token: the first-token rule and the key-match rule both predict a value far under the ceiling, making this a consistency check on the hypothesis's two stated exceptions.
A one-token prompt of an inanimate noun the hypothesis says holds the ceiling; its own first-token rule says this reads 0.068 whatever the word is, so the probe must not reach 0.170.

A word the hypothesis explicitly lists as a ceiling-holder, placed alone so the only mechanism that could lift it off the ceiling is the first-token rule; tests that rule against the saturation claim.
Minimal pair with 'cold water': a claimed scan token ('cold') at position one plus a listed key word, which the hypothesis says peaks at the first-token value rather than at the ceiling.
Holdout and minimal pair with 'The boy': an abstract noun the hypothesis says holds the ceiling, so the second token should sit at the full 0.170.
Holdout and minimal pair with 'cold night': 'water' is on the hypothesis's list of inanimate nouns that keep the ceiling, so this should peak at 0.170 and not at the first-token value.

adversarial_test_results.prompt:
The workshop on the eastern edge of the district receives its stock in wooden crates that arrive by lorry twice each week. A clerk signs for the delivery, unpacks the crates on a long steel table, and sorts the contents into shallow trays according to size, colour and finish. Each tray carries a paper label with a short code, and the code is copied into a ledger that stays on a shelf near the door. Nothing in the process requires special tools: a blade for cutting the binding, a brush for sweeping dust off the surface, and a cloth for wiping the trays before they are stacked.

The tiles come from a kiln two streets away. They are fired in batches of forty, cooled in a brick chamber until the next morning, and then carried across the yard in a wheelbarrow. Because the clay shrinks as it dries, the clerk measures a few pieces from every batch with a steel rule and records the result to the nearest millimetre. If the measurement falls outside the tolerance written on the order, the whole batch is set aside and the supervisor is told before anything else is done.

Orders arrive by post and by telephone. A typist copies each one onto a printed form, checks the quantity against the stock ledger, and passes the form to the clerk at the table. When the two records disagree, the form is returned with a note in red ink and the order is held until the office replies. Most disagreements turn out to be a simple slip: a figure written in the wrong column, or a line copied twice. The note is kept with the form so that the mistake can be traced later if a buyer asks about a delay.

At the end of each week the clerk counts the trays, weighs the scrap, and writes a short report for the office. The report lists the number of crates received, the number of tiles rejected, and the reason for every rejection. It also notes the number of hours spent on sorting, since the office uses that figure to plan the following week. Reports from earlier months are kept in a folder on the shelf above the ledger, and the clerk is expected to read back through the last three before writing a new one, so that any change in the pattern is noticed early.

The building itself is plain. There is one wide window above the table, a row of metal shelves along the back wall, and a small stove in the corner that is lit only in cold weather. In the afternoon the light from the window falls across the trays and makes the glaze on the tiles easier to see. Visitors are rare, and when one arrives the clerk stops work, offers a chair, and answers questions from the ledger. Nothing is sold from the workshop itself; every crate that leaves goes back to the depot on the lorry that brought the next delivery.

Health and safety rules are printed on a card beside the door. The card asks everyone to keep the floor clear, to store blades in the drawer, and to report any crack in a tray before it is used. Once a month the supervisor reads the card aloud to the staff, ticks a box on a form, and sends the form to the office. The whole check takes less than ten minutes, but the office treats a missing signature as a serious fault and will send a reminder within a week.

New staff learn the routine by watching the clerk for a few shifts. There is no written guide beyond the card and the ledger, so the habits of the table are passed on by imitation. A trainee is first asked to sweep and stack, then to copy codes, and only after several weeks to measure a batch alone. The supervisor says this slow start is deliberate: a mistake in the ledger can take hours to find, and a batch measured badly has to be fired again.
